videos.script: Some apps ask for your password to another service. Give it to them, and they can do anything you can, for as long as they like. {{password}} OAuth exists so that never has to happen. You are sent to the service itself, you agree to a short list there, and the app gets a token that does that list and nothing more. {{delegation}} In this lesson you run a small authorization server of your own, called idp.py. You drive it with curl, one request at a time, and you read every answer. {{curl}} Then come the pieces around it. A proof that makes a stolen code useless. Tokens for machines that act on their own. And tokens that renew themselves, and notice when a copy has been stolen. {{pieces}} OpenID Connect adds one thing on top of all that, which is who signed in. {{oidc}} SAML does the same job in signed XML, in the companies where you will meet it. You will sign an assertion, change one word in it, and watch the check fail. {{saml}} By the end you will know which of the three you are looking at, and what a defender checks in each. {{table}}
